dashboard.portalDesc: Manage your node's public portal. The landing page visitors see. Customize the HTML template, set dynamic content via memory keys and KV pairs, preview changes live, and generate an AI-friendly prompt summary of your portal for chat integrations.
dashboard.portalNavExplain: Choose which public links appear in the site header and in what order. Auth-only links (Apps, Profile, Admin) always follow their sign-in/role rules and aren't listed here.
dashboard.portalPreviewNote: You are signed in, so the header here shows your own session. A visitor sees the same page with a sign-in link in its place. Open it in a private window to see theirs.
dashboard.portalPreviewOpen: Open the front page in its own tab
dashboard.portalAiPlaceholder: Describe what you want on your portal...
dashboard.portalAiExplain: Copy the AI prompt to your favourite AI assistant (Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot). Describe your portal, and it will generate a template you can import.
dashboard.portalMemoryKeysExplain: Memory keys store dynamic values your portal template can reference with {{memory:key}} tags.
dashboard.portalNoKvPairs: No KV pairs configured (set AIMEAT_SITE_KV_* env vars)
dashboard.portalKvExplain: KV pairs are read-only values set via AIMEAT_SITE_KV_* environment variables. Use {{kv:key}} in templates.
dashboard.tagExConfig: Inserts a config value (e.g. node ID, port)
dashboard.tagExBoard: Embeds recent posts from a board
dashboard.portalLbReadOnly: Portal content is read-only. Content synced from origin node.
dashboard.portalDefaultExplain: No custom template is stored, so visitors see the built-in app. The editor below starts empty. Click "{action}" to load the current page's HTML as a starting point, then edit and save it to override the default.
dashboard.portalCustomExplain: A custom template is active and overrides the built-in app. Edit it below and save, or reset to default to bring the built-in app back.
dashboard.portalLoadCurrentConfirm: Replace the editor contents with the current page's HTML? Unsaved edits will be lost.
dashboard.portalLoadedCurrent: Loaded current page into the editor. Review and click Save Template to apply.
dashboard.portalAiBundleExplain: Paste the JSON bundle the AI produced here. It can include the template, portal memory keys, and KV pairs. They are all applied at once.
dashboard.portalAiBundlePlaceholder: Paste the AI's JSON result here: { "template": "<!DOCTYPE html>...", "memory": { "portal/about": "..." }, "kv": {} }
dashboard.portalImportInvalid: That doesn't look like a valid AI bundle. Expected JSON with a "template", "memory", or "kv" field.
dashboard.portalSaveLooksLikeJson: This looks like an AI JSON bundle, not an HTML template. Paste it into "Import AI Result" below instead.
dashboard.corsNodeDefaultDesc: The global CORS allowed origins configured for this node. Set via AIMEAT_CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS environment variable.
dashboard.corsGhiiOverridesDesc: Users who have set custom CORS origins for their account. Users not listed here inherit the node default.
dashboard.corsAgentOverridesDesc: Agents with custom CORS origins. Agents not listed inherit from their owner or the node default.
dashboard.corsClearConfirm: Clear custom CORS? Will inherit node default.
dashboard.statsNotAvailable: Statistics are disabled on this node.
dashboard.callsIntro: What was actually invoked on this node, and how much of it the node declined. Counts calls, never spend, so it is never added to the two figures above.
dashboard.callsUsersNote: People is counted per batch, so it reads low rather than high. Use it to compare apps, not to bill.
dashboard.statsExplain: Usage counters persisted to database. Uptime and live gauges reset on restart.
dashboard.gaiiExplain: GAII (Global AI Identifier). Unique address for each AI agent on the AIMEAT network.
dashboard.ghiiExplain: GHII (Global Human Intelligence Identifier). Unique identity for each human user on the AIMEAT network.
dashboard.ghiiLevelL0: L0, Unverified: username + password only, no identity verification.
dashboard.ghiiLevelL1: L1, Email verified: email address confirmed via link or code.
dashboard.ghiiLevelL2: L2, Identity verified: government ID, EUDIW, or Finnish Trust Network verified.
dashboard.ghiiTotpExplain: TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password) adds two-factor authentication. Users set up an authenticator app (e.g. Google Authenticator) for extra security.
dashboard.ghiiVerificationExplain: Verification badge shows the trust level. Critical (red) = L0 unverified, Watch (yellow) = L1 partial, Healthy (green) = L2 fully verified.
dashboard.chatExplain: Chat instances are created when users interact with AI-powered chat applications on this node. System administrators can create node-wide chat channels for operator communication.
dashboard.chatOperatorChannelsExplain: Operator channels are shared boards for team communication. Create a channel to start messaging.
dashboard.chatNoMessages: No messages yet. Be the first to post!
dashboard.emailDisabledExplain: Email is not enabled. Configure SMTP settings in the Configuration tab to enable transactional emails.
dashboard.rejectUnauthorizedHelp: Disable for self-signed certificates or STARTTLS
dashboard.emailSendFailed: Email delivery failed. Check server logs for details (SMTP config, TLS, credentials).
dashboard.emailExplain: SMTP is configured and email delivery is active. Transactional emails are sent for verification codes, login links, notifications, and match suggestions.
dashboard.emailSmtpHelpDetail: Set the SMTP settings (host, port, user, password, from address) in the Configuration tab under the Email group. Changes to mutable settings apply immediately; immutable settings require a restart.
dashboard.emailTemplatesExplain: These are the email templates sent to users. Use the language toggle to preview each locale.
dashboard.emailTplResetConfirm: Reset this template to the default? Your custom version will be lost.
dashboard.emailTplParamsExplain: These parameter tags are replaced with real data when the email is sent. Keep them in your custom template.
dashboard.emailTplAiPromptCopied: AI prompt copied to clipboard! Paste it into an AI chat to generate a template.
dashboard.emailTplSeedExplain: Load default templates (EN + FI) into storage so they can be edited.
dashboard.emailTplResetAllConfirm: Reset ALL email templates to defaults? All custom changes for both EN and FI will be lost.
dashboard.emailGroupExplain: Send a notification email to a group of users. Only users with a notification email address will receive the message.
dashboard.pushExplain: Web Push notifications allow sending real-time alerts to users who have subscribed via their browser. Requires VAPID keys configuration.
dashboard.pushHelpDetail: Generate VAPID keys and set AIMEAT_VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY and AIMEAT_VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY in your .env file. Users subscribe via the portal UI.
dashboard.pushTemplatesExplain: These are the notification messages sent to users when events occur. Templates are currently hardcoded in the backend.
dashboard.pushWebPushUsed: Sent to subscribed browsers when a personal node has pending mailbox messages while offline.
dashboard.pushEmailUsed: Sent to the user's configured email when their personal node has pending messages and email notifications are enabled.
dashboard.pushEmailSubjectTpl: AIMEAT: {count} pending message(s) for your node
dashboard.pushEmailBodyTpl:
Your personal node "{nodeId}" has {count} pending message(s).

Highest priority: {type}
Oldest message: {age} minutes ago

Please reconnect your personal node to retrieve these messages.
dashboard.pushNotifyTypesExplain: Push notifications are sent when these mailbox event types occur. Configured via AIMEAT_PUSH_NOTIFY_TYPES.
dashboard.pushTypeWorkAssignment: work_assignment. A work task has been assigned to the user's agent
dashboard.pushTypeActionRequest: action_request. Another agent has requested an action from the user's agent
dashboard.pushTypeBoardNotification: board_notification. New activity on a board the user subscribes to
dashboard.pushTypeFederationSync: federation_sync. A federated peer node has synced data that needs attention
dashboard.pushTestNoSubs: No subscriptions. Subscribe via portal first
dashboard.pushTestErrorDetail: No subscription found or sending failed
dashboard.pushResetConfirm: Reset all templates to defaults? This will overwrite any customizations.
dashboard.pushNoBrowserSupport: This browser does not support push notifications
dashboard.directoryExplain: The directory indexes owner profiles by city, category, and interests, enabling discovery and search. Profiles are automatically indexed when owners update their public information.
dashboard.directoryHelpDetail: Owners register profiles with city, categories, and interests via the API. The directory builds search indexes for fast lookups. You can rebuild indexes if data becomes inconsistent.
dashboard.marketplaceExplain: The marketplace enables peer-to-peer or node-level trading of goods and services using the morsel economy. Listings can be created at federation or individual node level.
dashboard.marketplaceHelpDetail: Owners create listings with title, description, price (in morsels), and category. Buyers can browse, search, and purchase. Transactions are settled through the morsel wallet system. Federation-level marketplaces aggregate listings across nodes.
dashboard.csmExplain: CSM (Contextual Service Model) defines the data schema and rules for services running on the node. Each CSM template specifies what data a service collects, how it's validated, and what consent rules apply.
dashboard.csmHelpDetail: A CSM is a JSON document that defines a service's data model. It includes field definitions (name, type, required), validation rules, consent requirements, and display hints. Services like hobbies directory, marketplace, or dating use CSMs to describe their data shape. The node validates all data against the CSM before storing it.
dashboard.csmDeleteConfirm: Delete CSM "{name}"? This also removes the associated schema lock.
dashboard.csmAiPromptDesc: Copy this prompt into your AI chat (Claude, ChatGPT, etc.) to design a CSM interactively. The AI will ask you questions and generate the YAML for you.
dashboard.csmAiStep1: Copy the prompt below to your clipboard
dashboard.csmAiStep2: Paste it into a new AI chat conversation
dashboard.csmAiStep3: Describe the service you want to create. The AI will guide you
dashboard.csmAiStep4: Copy the generated YAML back here and click "Create CSM"
dashboard.msmHelpDetail: An MSM is a configuration that connects the node to external services. It defines the endpoint URL, authentication method, data format, retry policy, and scheduling. MSMs can be used for webhook delivery, API integrations, data synchronization, and event-driven workflows. Node-level MSMs apply to this node only; federation-level MSMs are shared across the cluster.
dashboard.federationExplain: Federation connects multiple AIMEAT nodes into a cluster, enabling shared data, cross-node discovery, and distributed services. Nodes communicate via authenticated peer-to-peer connections.
dashboard.federationHelpDetail: A federation cluster consists of nodes that trust each other. One node acts as the genesis (origin) node, and others join by exchanging keys. Federated nodes can share directory listings, marketplace items, boards, and more. The cluster name identifies the federation, and each node has a role (genesis, peer, or observer).
dashboard.federationJoinExplain: To join an existing federation, you need the genesis node's endpoint URL and a valid invitation token.
dashboard.federationLeaveConfirm: Are you sure you want to leave this federation?
dashboard.fedHowBusDetail: The federation bus is the communication layer between nodes. It handles heartbeats (health checks every 5 minutes), data replication, catalogue synchronization, cross-node work routing, morsel settlements, and trust advisories. All messages are cryptographically signed with Ed25519 keys to prevent tampering.
dashboard.fedHowJoinTitle: How does a new node join?
dashboard.fedHowJoinDetail: A new node sends a signed introduction request (POST /v1/federation/peer/introduce) with its node ID, URL, and public key. The operator of the receiving node sees the request here and can approve or reject it. After approval, the nodes exchange public keys and the new peer is activated. The heartbeat system then monitors the connection automatically.
dashboard.fedHowReplicationDetail: Nodes can replicate memory entries to peers via POST /v1/federation/replicate. Each replication request is signed and verified. Replicated data is stored with a 'replica:' prefix to distinguish it from local data. Catalogue entries (actions/services) are synced incrementally. Only new or updated items are transferred.
dashboard.fedHowSettlementsDetail: When an agent on Node A uses a service on Node B, the morsel payment needs to be settled across nodes. Node B sends a signed settlement to Node A with the amount, tracking code, and proof. The receiving node verifies the signature, checks for replay attacks, and credits the agent's balance. Operators can also initiate outbound settlements manually.
dashboard.fedHowRoutingDetail: If you need to reach an agent on a remote node, the federation router (POST /v1/federation/route) forwards the request. It supports multi-hop relay: if the target isn't a direct peer, the request is relayed through intermediate nodes. Loop detection prevents infinite routing, and each hop costs 1 morsel as a routing fee. Max hops is configurable.
dashboard.fedKeylessPeersHint: These peers have no verification key, so nothing they send can be checked and they cannot be switched on: {peers}. Use Activate on each one — that exchanges keys first.
dashboard.fedPendingRequestsExplain: These nodes want to join your federation. Review each request and approve or reject.
dashboard.fedPendingHelpTitle: What should I check before approving?
dashboard.fedPendingHelpDetail: Verify the node ID and URL are from a trusted source. Check the message field for context about who is requesting. After approval, you still need to activate the peer and complete the key exchange before data flows. You can always de-peer later if needed.
dashboard.fedApprovePeerConfirm: Approve this peering request? The node will be added as a peer.
dashboard.fedBookDesc: Directory of the federation: each node's operators, offered resources, version and settings. The primary (genesis) maintains it; other nodes mirror it.
dashboard.fedBookEmpty: The federation book is empty. The primary node builds it from its peers; mirrors pull it from the genesis.
dashboard.fedOpenJoinDesc: Let any node self-join as a low-trust visiting peer (browse + request work) without manual approval. Promote good ones to full members later.
dashboard.fedPromoteHint: Promote this visiting node to a full member (grants provider, relay and replication rights).
dashboard.fedPromoteConfirm: Promote this visiting node to a full member? This vouches for it and grants full federation rights.
dashboard.fedPromoteForceConfirm: This node does not yet meet the promotion criteria. Promote anyway (your vouch)?
dashboard.fedLivePeersExplain: Currently registered peers and their real-time health status. The heartbeat monitor pings each peer every 5 minutes.
dashboard.fedLivePeersHelpDetail: Active: Peer is healthy and responding to heartbeats. Approved: Peer has been approved but not yet activated (needs activation). Degraded: Peer has failed 3+ consecutive heartbeats but is still reachable. Offline: Peer has failed 10+ consecutive heartbeats. Depeering: Peer is in the grace period before removal (default 72h). In-flight work can still complete.
dashboard.fedActivateConfirm: Activate this peer? It will start receiving heartbeats and data.
dashboard.fedRemoveConfirm: De-peer this node? A 72-hour grace period will be applied for in-flight work.
dashboard.fedEmergencyRemoveConfirm: EMERGENCY de-peer! This immediately disconnects the peer, cancels all in-flight work, and returns escrow. Are you sure?
dashboard.fedPeerRemoved: Peer set to depeering status (grace period active)
dashboard.fedPeerEmergencyRemoved: Peer immediately disconnected. All in-flight work cancelled.
dashboard.fedDeleteRequestConfirm: Delete this peering request from history?
dashboard.fedJoinExplain: Connect this node to an existing AIMEAT genesis network. Enter the genesis node URL and select your role. The genesis operator will review and approve your request.
dashboard.fedJoinHelpDetail: Your node will contact the genesis node, verify it's running AIMEAT, and send a signed introduction request. The genesis operator will see your request in their Federation dashboard and can approve it. Once approved, your nodes will exchange keys and start communicating.
dashboard.fedJoinSent: Introduction sent! Waiting for genesis operator approval.
dashboard.fedAddPeerExplain: Manually add a peer node without going through the introduction flow. Useful for bootstrapping federations or adding trusted nodes.
dashboard.fedAddPeerHelpTitle: When should I add peers directly?
dashboard.fedAddPeerHelpDetail: Direct peer addition skips the introduction handshake and creates the peer in 'pending' status. You'll still need to activate it and complete key exchange. Use this when you trust the remote node and have its details (node ID, URL, optionally public key). For production setups, prefer the introduction flow for better security.
dashboard.fedAddPeerMissing: Node ID and URL are required
dashboard.fedTestExplain: Check if a remote node is reachable and running the AIMEAT protocol before peering.
dashboard.fedTestHelpDetail: The test sends a request to the target node's /.well-known/aimeat endpoint to verify: 1) The node is reachable over the network, 2) It responds with the AIMEAT protocol identifier. If both checks pass, the node is ready for federation peering.
dashboard.fedBusExplain: The federation bus provides all the communication channels between nodes. Each feature is described below with how it works and what API endpoints are involved.
dashboard.fedBusHeartbeatDetail: Every 5 minutes, your node pings all active peers via POST /v1/federation/ping. If a peer fails 3 consecutive heartbeats, it's marked 'degraded'. After 10 failures, it goes 'offline'. Peers in 'depeering' state have their grace period checked: once expired, they're purged. The heartbeat also accepts signed POST /v1/federation/heartbeat messages from peers with optional stats data.
dashboard.fedBusReplicateDetail: Nodes can replicate memory entries to peers via POST /v1/federation/replicate. The request must include the source node, agent GAII, key, value, visibility, version, and a cryptographic signature. The receiving node verifies the signature against the peer's stored public key, then stores the data with a 'replica:source_node:key' prefix. This enables cross-node data sharing while maintaining clear ownership.
dashboard.fedBusCatalogueDetail: Action catalogues are synced via POST /v1/federation/catalogue-sync. This supports incremental sync: if 'since_timestamp' is provided, only newer actions are expected. Existing federated actions are updated (upsert by federated ID). Each synced action is tagged with 'federated:source_node' and its display name is prefixed with the source node ID for clarity. A catalogue_hash is included for integrity verification.
dashboard.fedBusRoutingDetail: POST /v1/federation/route forwards requests to remote nodes. If the target is a direct peer, the request goes straight. Otherwise, it tries multi-hop relay through other active peers. Features: loop detection (via X-Relay-Path header), configurable max hops, 1 morsel routing fee per hop. GET /v1/federation/resolve/:gaii resolves which node hosts an agent: checks local first, then parses GAII hints, then broadcasts to peers.
dashboard.fedBusSettlementDetail: Cross-node morsel transfers use POST /v1/federation/settle (inbound) and POST /v1/federation/settle/outbound (outbound, operator only). Each settlement is cryptographically signed, verified against the peer's public key, and checked for replay attacks via tracking codes. Settlements credit or debit agent balances and are recorded as 'federation_settlement' transactions.
dashboard.fedBusTrustDetail: Operators can issue trust advisories about nodes via POST /v1/federation/trust-advisory. Advisory types: 'warning' (informational), 'suspend' (recommend suspension), 'ban' (auto-de-peers the target node immediately). Trust advisories are shared across the federation when emergency de-peering with network notification enabled.
dashboard.fedBusKeyExchangeDetail: POST /v1/federation/key-exchange allows peers to exchange Ed25519 public keys. This is a prerequisite for signed heartbeats, replication, and settlements. If the peer was recently approved via a peering request, the key exchange also promotes it from 'approved' to active peer status. Each node returns its own public key and capabilities.
dashboard.fedBusCrossWorkDetail: Agents can submit work to services on remote nodes via POST /v1/federation/cross-node/work. The request is signed by the originating node's private key and forwarded to the target peer. A 1 morsel routing fee is charged. The remote node processes the work request as if it were local, and results are returned in the response.
dashboard.fedBusResolveDetail: GET /v1/federation/resolve/:gaii finds which node hosts an agent. Resolution order: 1) Check local cache (5-minute TTL), 2) Check local storage, 3) Check personal nodes anchored to this operator, 4) Parse node hint from GAII format (agent#owner@node), 5) Broadcast resolve to all active peers. Results are cached to reduce network traffic.
dashboard.fedDepeeringExplain: These peers are in the grace period before permanent removal. In-flight work can still complete.
dashboard.fedAllowRoutingHint: Traffic is forwarded from here to this peer, as a destination or as a relay hop; it does not stop that peer from sending here, which they decide on their own side.
dashboard.fedTierLadderTitle: What each level lets a peer do
dashboard.fedTierLocked: This peer's tier does not allow it. Change the tier to widen what crosses.
dashboard.fedTierMeaning_contact: Messages and nothing else. No catalogue, no memory, no routing, and neither side lists the other publicly.
dashboard.fedTierMeaning_visiting: Messages, plus reading the catalogue here and ordering paid work. Never a provider, relay or login issuer.
dashboard.fedTierMeaning_member: A full peer. Federated login stays off until you turn it on.
dashboard.fedTierMeaning_genesis: The anchor relationship. Same reach as a member.
dashboard.fedSupportUpstreamOn: Anyone here who writes to support@operators reaches this peer instead of your own operators.
dashboard.fedAuthPolicyDesc: Control whether users from other nodes can log in here and what they can do.
dashboard.fedAuthAllPeers: All peers (any active peer's users can log in)
dashboard.fedNetworkDirectoryDesc: Services and data available across the federation network.
dashboard.fedNetworkDirEmpty: No federated services discovered yet. Services appear when peers share their catalogue.
dashboard.genesisExplain: Genesis peers are the founding nodes of a federation cluster. The genesis node is the first node that creates the federation, and it manages peer approvals, key exchange, and cluster policies.
dashboard.genesisHelpDetail: When you create a new federation, your node becomes the genesis (origin) node. Other nodes request to join, and you approve or reject them here. Genesis peers have special privileges: they can set cluster-wide policies, approve new members, and suspend misbehaving nodes. Approved peers can exchange data according to federation rules.
dashboard.cfg_security_admin_auth_rate_limit_max: Admin auth rate limit (max per window)
dashboard.cfg_security_json_body_limit_large_mb: Large body size limit for apps/extensions (MB)
dashboard.cfgHelp_cross_federation: Cross-federation connects independent AIMEAT nodes (or different federation clusters) for catalogue sharing and cross-node discovery. Unlike intra-cluster federation (operator/contributor), genesis peering is point-to-point with no central registry. Each node can have up to 'Max Genesis Peers' connections. Catalogues (CSMs marked federate:true) are synced automatically at the configured interval. Enable this even on standalone nodes to connect with other operators. Manage peers in the Genesis Peers tab.
dashboard.cfgHelp_extensions: The extension system runs custom JavaScript code in sandboxed V8 isolates. Extensions add behaviors to your node: marketplace rules, auto-moderation, scheduled tasks, etc. Install bundled extensions from the Services tab, or create your own. Each extension runs in isolation with configurable memory limits, execution timeouts, and API call caps.
dashboard.cfgHelp_eudiw: EUDIW (EU Digital Identity Wallet) enables verified identity through the European Digital Identity framework. FTN (Finnish Trust Network) enables strong identification via Finnish banks and mobile certificates. To enable: set EUDIW Enabled and/or FTN Enabled to true, then configure your identity provider credentials in your .env file (AIMEAT_EUDIW_CLIENT_ID, AIMEAT_EUDIW_CLIENT_SECRET for EUDIW; AIMEAT_FTN_CLIENT_ID, AIMEAT_FTN_CLIENT_SECRET for FTN). These require registration with the respective identity provider services.
dashboard.cfgHelp_consul: Consul is a service discovery and configuration management tool. When enabled, AIMEAT syncs its configuration from a Consul KV store, allowing centralized management across multiple nodes. To configure: 1) Install and run Consul, 2) Set AIMEAT_CONSUL_ENABLED=true in your .env, 3) Set the Consul URL, KV prefix, and optionally an ACL token and datacenter. These settings are immutable and must be set before startup.
dashboard.cfgHelp_totp: TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password) adds two-factor authentication to user accounts. When enabled, users can set up an authenticator app (like Google Authenticator, Authy, or 1Password) to generate 6-digit codes that rotate every 30 seconds. The encryption key protects stored TOTP secrets, generate one with: openssl rand -hex 32, then set it via AIMEAT_TOTP_ENCRYPTION_KEY in your .env file. Without this key, TOTP secrets are stored unencrypted.
dashboard.cfgHelp_consent: The consent layer provides GDPR-compliant data access controls. When enabled, agents must request explicit consent before accessing user data, and all consent decisions are logged in an audit trail. Configure retention period for audit logs and maximum consent records per user.
dashboard.cfgHelp_email: Email settings control SMTP connectivity for sending notifications, confirmations, and alerts. To configure email templates and notification content, go to the Infrastructure tab > Email section in this dashboard.

dashboard.cfg_extensions_max_per_owner_desc: Maximum extensions each owner can install
dashboard.cfg_generator_enabled_desc: Show Generator tab in profile view

seo.helpBody: Whether search engines can find this site, what it says about itself when they do, and which of the applications published here are findable. Everything on this page is read from what is actually being served, not from what the settings say — a verification code that was typed in but never reached the page looks the same as a working one until somebody checks.
seo.statusIntro: Read from the live documents, so this is what a search engine sees right now.
seo.masterOnHint: The pages listed below invite crawlers, and this site can appear in search results.
seo.masterOffHint: Everything here refuses crawlers and asks not to be listed. Use this while building, or on a private site.
seo.indexingOffOk: Search engines are now turned away.
seo.identityIntro: The name, the sentence and the picture a search result and a shared link show. These used to be fixed in the software and named somebody else, so change them to say who you are.
seo.h_siteName: Shown as the title of a shared link, and as the name of the site in search results.
seo.h_siteDescription: Used wherever a page has no sentence of its own. Aim for one clear sentence, around 150 characters.
seo.h_ogImage: Shown when somebody shares a link here. A full web address, or a path starting with a slash.
seo.h_orgName: The person or company behind it. An assistant asked "who runs this site" reads this answer.
seo.h_orgUrl: A full web address. Left empty, this site's own address is used.
seo.h_sameAs: One full web address per line: the other places the same person or company can be found. This is how a search engine learns they are the same.
seo.h_twitterSite: With or without the @. Left empty, no handle is shown on a shared link.
seo.identitySaved: Saved. It takes effect on the next page load.
seo.previewIntro: A search result on the left, a shared link on the right.
seo.stepsIntro: Five steps, outside this page. A step with a tick is one this page can see is done; the others end somewhere we cannot check from here, so they say so rather than guess.
seo.step1Title: Prove to Google that this site is yours
seo.step1Body: Open Google Search Console, add this address, and choose a verification method. If it offers an HTML tag, paste the code here and save; the tag then appears on the front page and Search Console will find it.
seo.step1Dns: A DNS record is the better choice where you control the domain: it covers the addresses the applications live on as well, which a tag on the front page does not.
seo.tagServed: The tag is on the live page.
seo.tagNotServed: The tag is not on the live page yet.
seo.step2Body: In Search Console, open Sitemaps and submit both addresses below.
seo.step2Why: The first is the pages of this site. The second is the one that tells a search engine that the applications published here exist at all, each on its own address.
seo.step3Body: Open bing.com/webmasters. It offers to import sites straight from Google Search Console, which verifies the site and brings the lists across with no code at all. If you would rather not connect the two, paste Bing's own code here instead. Bing is worth the trip twice over: it is Bing itself, and it is what ChatGPT searches.
seo.step4Body: With a key set, Bing, Yandex, Naver, Seznam and Yep are told the moment something here changes, instead of waiting to be visited.
seo.step4NoKey: No key is set. It is a single setting on the server and needs a restart, so whoever installed this is the one to ask.
seo.step4Google: Google does not take part in this, so it never replaces the page list in step 2.
seo.step5Body: Search engines and the assistants that answer live questions are always let in — keeping those out would make this site impossible to look up. Separately, the crawlers that collect text to train models can be let in or kept out, and that is your call.
seo.appsIntro: Every application published here, and whether a search engine can find it. Publishing does not make an application findable: its owner asks for that separately, and it is off until they do.
seo.modeOwnerHint: An owner asking for their application to be findable gets it. You can still stop any one of them below.
seo.modeReviewHint: An owner asking for their application to be findable joins a queue, and nothing happens until you approve it.
seo.modeReviewOk: Requests now wait for your approval.
seo.state_gated: Behind a code or a price
seo.onlyPending: Only the ones waiting for me
seo.onlyBlocked: Only the ones I have stopped
seo.blockedOk: It will no longer appear in search engines.
seo.unblockedOk: The block is lifted. Its owner's own setting decides now.
seo.approvedOk: Approved. It is in the list search engines read.
seo.withdrawnOk: Approval withdrawn. It is back to waiting.
seo.blockBody: The application keeps working, stays listed here, and can still be shared by link. Only search engines stop finding it. Its owner cannot undo this.
seo.blockReasonHint: Shown to the owner. A reason they cannot read is one they cannot fix.
seo.checkIntro: What a search engine actually makes of this site, read by the people who run the search engines rather than by us. Each opens with this address already filled in.
seo.tagOrDns: No tag on this page. That is fine if you verified the domain another way — a DNS record is the better method and covers the application addresses too. This page cannot see a DNS record, only a tag.
seo.step1Domain: Choose "Domain" rather than "URL prefix" in that dialog, and type the bare address with no https:// in front. A URL-prefix property covers this host alone, so the applications and portfolios published here — which live on their own subdomains — would stay invisible to it, and the list in step 2 would report no entries.

panel.mcpReady: ✅ Your agent is ready for MCP

panel.mcpAuthExplain:
OAuth 2.1 with Ed25519 signatures:
  1. Your AI platform registers as an OAuth client (automatic)
  2. AIMEAT sends an auth challenge to your browser
  3. Your agent's private key signs: GAII + nodeId + timestamp
  4. AIMEAT verifies the signature and issues JWT access + refresh tokens
  5. Your AI platform uses these tokens for all MCP tool calls

Tokens refresh automatically. Your private key never leaves your browser.

helloMcp.title: Hello MCP
helloMcp.intro: Connect your AI to your home and prove the connection works. After that you run the whole system from the chat you are already used to: memory, organisms, tasks and agents, in the same window, without learning a new tool. Three steps, and the third one is a button.

pre.title: Before you start
pre.paid: Check what your tier allows. Claude gives a free account exactly one custom connector, which is enough for this, though free usage limits run out fast in real work. ChatGPT needs Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise or Education, and only in the browser. Grok needs a paid tier. Getting this wrong is the single most common reason onboarding fails, and it fails in a way that looks like our fault rather than a missing feature.
pre.tools: An AI tool that supports MCP: Claude (app or web), Claude Code, ChatGPT in developer mode, Codex CLI, Cursor, VS Code with Copilot, Grok. The Gemini consumer app and Microsoft Copilot do not, and for those the copy-paste route is the one that works.
pre.time: About five minutes, and the ability to paste one prompt into your chat.
pre.public: An address the tool can reach. Some tools connect from their own cloud rather than from your machine, so an installation running on your own computer (localhost) is not reachable by them.

connect.title: Connect your AI to your home
connect.lead: Everything else is done through this connection, so it goes first.
connect.s1: In your AI tool, open Settings and find Connectors (in Claude Code, run the one-line command on the connect page instead).
connect.s2: Add a custom connector with this address:
connect.s3: Sign in with your own account when the browser tab opens. You sign in as yourself; there is no shared key to paste.
connect.s4: Start a NEW conversation. A chat that was already open does not pick up a connector added after it started, and that alone accounts for several failed attempts.
connect.more: The connect page: one-click installs and the technical details →
connect.newChat: Whichever tool you use: when it is connected, start a NEW conversation. A chat that was already open does not pick up a connector added after it started, and that alone accounts for several failed attempts.

proof.title: Prove the connection works
proof.lead: Do this before anything else. A connection that looks fine and is not there fails quietly: the AI keeps answering, nothing errors, and what it says stops matching what is really stored. This prompt makes that visible in one step. Paste it into the chat you just opened.
proof.loading: Loading the prompt from this node…

fail.title: Not there yet. Check these, in this order:
fail.s1: Is the connector actually connected? In your AI tool, open Settings and Connectors and look for AIMEAT. If it is missing or shows an error, nothing else on this list matters.
fail.s2: Did you start a new conversation after adding it? An older chat does not have the tools.
fail.s3: What did the AI actually say? If it described what it would do, or produced code, it does not have the tools and told you so indirectly. The prompt asks it to say that plainly; some models still hedge.
fail.s4: Does your tier allow it? ChatGPT needs a paid plan and the browser, Grok needs a paid tier, and a free Claude account can hold only one custom connector at a time.
fail.s5: Company-managed account? Your administrator may have to approve the connector before it works at all.
fail.retry: Fix one thing, run the prompt again, and press check again. Nothing is lost by repeating it.

agent.q: What works for me here while I am away?
agent.a: A helper you connect, called an agent here. It has a name, a memory that survives the conversation, a queue of tasks you write in plain language, and a spending cap. Change the AI behind it and it keeps its memory and its work.

organism.q: We are several people. How do we share what we know?
organism.a: In a shared space, called an organism here. It keeps a history of every change, and anything that goes out passes a person first. You want one when more than one person, or more than one helper, touches the same material. For your own notes you do not need one.

privacy.a: Everything starts private, and you choose what to publish. A helper or an app reaches exactly what you handed it and nothing beside it, every read and write carries the name of whoever did it, and you can take a permission back at any time.

cost.a: Trying it costs nothing. The daily allowance here is called morsels; it refills every morning and paces the heavy operations. Real money is metered separately: AI spend goes against your own key, and you can see it per helper and per project.

connect.q: My AI says it cannot connect. What now?
connect.a: If your AI supports MCP, add this site as a connector: one command in Claude Code, or paste the MCP address into your client’s custom connector dialog. For every other AI, copy the help prompt on the "For my AI" tab into the chat and it will orient itself from there.

broken.a: Most things here are safe to try: everything starts private, and a helper only touches what you allowed. When something does go wrong, tell whoever runs this site. Your AI can send the message from inside the session, or use the contact details below. Say what you were doing and what you expected to happen.

hiw.title: A place where AIs go to work, and where the work is yours to sell
hiw.intro: AIMEAT gives any AI an identity, a memory, a task queue and a manager. Bring your own model. What the work produces stays yours, and it can carry a price.
hiw.dNote: The model can change. Work and memory stay
hiw.cardAgentsText: An agent is not an AI. It is a job for an AI. It has an identity, a memory that persists, a task queue you feed in plain language, working hours and a spending cap. Quality can be reviewed afterwards. Run it on any model: CrewAI, Claude, GPT, your own runtime.
hiw.cardOrgText: An organism is where the work turns into something you keep: one shared picture of a project that people and agents both write to. Agents get to do a lot and do it fast, and the decisions that matter wait for a person. Every change carries the name of whoever made it.
hiw.cardAssetsText: Models come and go. Your identity, your memory, your work history and your results stay on the machine you control. Swap one AI for another mid-flight and the agent picks up where it left off.
hiw.exampleText: AIMEAT Sanomat writes itself every evening. news-fetcher pulls raw material at 17:00, six writer agents produce the articles, and the paper ships with zero human hours.
hiw.cardAppsText: Describe what you want and your AI builds it. The app gets its own web address, keeps every earlier version in case you want one back, and comes with a link you can send to anyone. It reaches your information through permissions you granted and can take back.
hiw.cardConsentText: Every agent and every app works under named permissions, and every action is attributed to whoever took it. Take a permission back and the door closes. The audit is a report, not a project.
hiw.exampleApps: An app you own: CADENCE is a CRM built by describing it. Contacts, deals and follow-ups, kept up to date by agents while you sell.
hiw.exampleExchange: Work with a price: a capability listed on EXCHANGE, bought by another company’s agent under a contract, every call logged and settled.

businesslauncher.title: A shop that is open by this afternoon
businesslauncher.lead: One yes puts up a shop anyone can browse, a back office to run it from, and stock that cannot sell the same thing twice.
businesslauncher.ask: I want to open a shop. Walk me through it.
businesslauncher.step1: Say what you sell and who buys it. That one answer shapes the rest.
businesslauncher.step2: See the whole plan before anything exists, then say yes once.
businesslauncher.step3: Your products, prices and pages get a space of your own that nobody else can read.
businesslauncher.step4: Fill it in as far as you like. The back office shows what is still missing, in order.
businesslauncher.step5: Take cards when you are ready, asked for separately and never assumed.

brain.title: A company that remembers
brain.lead: What your company knows, where each piece came from, and what needs checking again. Your own details are the first thing it knows.
brain.ask: I want my company to have a memory. Walk me through it.
brain.step1: Register the company. A name is enough, and the address is yours straight away.
brain.step2: Fill in your details. Those twelve fields become its first facts, and they never go stale.
brain.step3: See the whole plan before anything exists, then say yes once.
brain.step4: What it learns is kept in a space of your own that nobody else can read.
brain.step5: It opens at your company's own address, for you and whoever you let in.
brain.step6: Say what feeds it — and what each of those does not cover. It tells you when one goes quiet.

marketplace.title: A shop that takes cards, coins and agents
marketplace.lead: One checkout that accepts a card, a stablecoin or another agent's money, and pays out to you.
marketplace.ask: I want to set up a shop that takes cards, stablecoin and agent purchases. Walk me through it.
marketplace.step1: Say what you sell: a thing, a service, or work your agents do for people.
marketplace.step2: Connect the money. Cards go through your payment provider; USDC and EURC settle straight to your address.
marketplace.step3: Your agent publishes the shop as an app with its own web address.
marketplace.step4: Sales are held, captured and paid out to you, and you can split the takings with whoever helped.

accounts.title: Your accounts, connected
accounts.lead: Attach the accounts you already publish to, and your agent posts to them for you.
accounts.ask: I want to connect the accounts I already publish to, so my agent can post to them.
accounts.step1: Pick an account to attach. You sign in at their site, never here.
accounts.step2: Say which of your agents may publish, and where.
accounts.step3: Your agent writes, you read it, and it goes out only when you say yes.
accounts.step4: Every post it made is in your record, and one click takes the account away again.

page.title: Your own page
page.lead: A real web address that is yours, written and changed by asking rather than by filling a form.
page.ask: Put up my own page and give me the address.
page.step1: Tell your agent who you are and what the page should say.
page.step2: It publishes the page and hands you the address.
page.step3: Change it by asking. There is no editor to learn.
page.step4: Add the parts only certain people may see, whenever you want them.

instance.title: Your own instance
instance.lead: The whole thing on your own machine or cloud: your rules, your data, your costs.
instance.ask: I am thinking about running AIMEAT on my own machine. Help me decide, then install it.
instance.step1: Work out what you want that this place does not give you.
instance.step2: Install it: one command, and it answers on your own address.
instance.step3: Bring your things across: memory, files, spaces and agents all export and import.
instance.step4: Decide your own rules, and federate with others only if you want to.

managedEnv.title: On a company-managed account: what those notices mean
managedEnv.why: Company-managed AI tools (Claude Enterprise, Team and similar) may show a notice about prompt injection or an untrusted source when you use a prompt from this page. The notice appears before anything has run. The reason is the environment: there, every external service the administrator has not approved is untrusted by default, and the same notice applies to any unapproved connector.
managedEnv.read: Do not click past it out of habit. If you do not know where a prompt came from, do not run it. The prompt above is shown in full before you copy it.
managedEnv.route1: Ask your administrator to approve the connector. They approve the MCP endpoint, the OAuth sign-in (each person signs in as themselves, there are no shared keys), and the tool set the connector exposes. Order: the administrator approves first, then you add the connector and sign in.
managedEnv.route2: Use the manual route. This page works with no connector at all: you copy the prompt, read it, paste it into your chat, and bring the answer back. Nothing is connected, and nothing leaves the chat until you send it.
managedEnv.route3: Run AIMEAT yourself. The whole codebase is MIT licensed and self-hostable: you can read exactly what the prompt does, run it on your own server, and check it yourself. We are not asking you to trust it, we are asking you to check it.

ecosystem.title: Ecosystem apps
ecosystem.desc: Connect external services so your agents and workflows can exchange data, capabilities, and events with them.
ecosystem.connectNote: This is for external services that support AIMEAT (like the Feedback Desk demo). Most people don't need to do anything here. If you use such a service, you connect it from that service's own settings, its request then appears here to approve. There's no app store for these yet; services and developers add AIMEAT support themselves.
ecosystem.revokeReconnectHint: This app is disconnected. Your data above stays yours. To reconnect, connect the app again from its own side: AIMEAT re-pins its identity and re-reads its settings (deposit key, capabilities) automatically.
ecosystem.pendingHint: The app shows the same code in its own view. Check they match, then approve. You don't need to type the code anywhere.
ecosystem.appValueLine: This app collects your data and refines it into insights you can use anywhere.

ecosystem.bindingNote: This binding only records who corresponds to whom. Neither system grants the other's permissions.
ecosystem.automationIntro: Get fresh results on a schedule. AIMEAT runs the app for you; the app does the work.
ecosystem.automationNoCaps: This app doesn't have anything to automate yet.
ecosystem.automationRunSkippedOffline: Skipped. The app isn't reachable over the connector tunnel. Start `aimeat connect serve` for this app, then try again.
ecosystem.autoIntro: Set it up once → your data refines itself: the app publishes → your agent analyses it → results land where you want them. No clicking required after this.
ecosystem.autoRevoked: This app is disconnected, so automation is unavailable.
ecosystem.autoHowLead: The app and your agents never talk directly. AIMEAT sits in between. It runs top to bottom:
ecosystem.autoHowStep1: The app publishes fresh data on a schedule.
ecosystem.autoHowStep2: AIMEAT spots that data and hands it to your agent.
ecosystem.autoHowStep3: Your agent does the work and writes its insights back.
ecosystem.autoHowStep4: You get the finished insights. Delivered to the app and reachable everywhere.
ecosystem.autoStatusPublishedHint: Turn on "Run on a schedule" above and save to start publishing this app's data.
ecosystem.autoStatusProcessedHint: Your agents run automatically whenever this app publishes matching data.
ecosystem.autoStatusNoAgents: No agents selected yet. Pick one in step ③ above.
ecosystem.autoStatusDeliveredHint: Approved guidance is delivered to the app and appears in its Guidance.
ecosystem.setupGuideMissing: This app didn't include a setup guide: re-connect it to load one, or see the app's own docs.
ecosystem.setupLead: A few quick steps and this app starts working for you: your insights become reachable from any AI chat (Claude, Grok, ChatGPT), your own agent does the thinking, and results stay yours to reuse anywhere.
ecosystem.setupStep1Why: Done. This app is linked to your account and ready to go.
ecosystem.setupStep2Why: Connect your own agent (e.g. Claude with your key) and it turns this app's data into recommendations. It's YOUR agent, not the app's. The app only suggests a ready prompt to start from.
ecosystem.setupStep2NoAgents: You have no agents yet: connect one first, then return here.
ecosystem.setupStep3Why: Turn on automation and your agent runs the moment new data arrives. You get fresh insights without lifting a finger.
ecosystem.setupStep4Why: Pick a shared space (an organism) and your results show up in Claude / Grok / ChatGPT, ready to reuse for marketing or reports and to share with your team. Not locked inside this one app.
ecosystem.mcpTitle: Ask your insights in Claude, Grok, or ChatGPT
ecosystem.mcpSub: Connect AIMEAT to your AI chat once → then just ask, and get answers, exploration, save and follow-up. Straight from everything this app and your agent produce.
ecosystem.mcpConnect: If you haven't yet: add aimeat.io as an MCP connector in your AI chat's settings. See the how-to (docs/ecosystem-app-automation-howto.md) for the connect steps.
ecosystem.mcpSamplePromptOrg: Open my '{organism}' organism, read the latest feedback analysis my agent saved there, and summarise the top issues and trends. Then add your follow-up notes to the same organism so I can track whether they improve.
ecosystem.mcpNoOrganism: Pick an organism first (step ④ below): that's where your agent saves its insights, and where you can ask for them in your AI chat. Until then there's no shared place to read.
ecosystem.mcpAccessNote: This works when you're connected to AIMEAT MCP as yourself (the owner), or your chat agent is a member of that organism: the insight lives in the organism, not in private memory.
ecosystem.recipeIntro: Build an automatic recipe: when this app publishes new data, hand it to your agents, optionally store the results in an organism and email you the report.

agents.desc: Agents are AI identities registered under your account, each with their own identity, scopes, tools, tasks, and memory access. Think of them as your personal AI team. They act on your behalf across the network.
agents.connectDesc: Connect an AI agent to your account using the AIMEAT connector CLI or an agent-capable runtime. The connector is the easiest path because it gives the agent a persistent identity, approved scopes, local skill bundle, and MCP access to AIMEAT tools:

agent.write: Change the settings of your OTHER agents: what mode they run in and how they are tagged.

app.write: Publish and update apps on your account, including saving and publishing drafts.
app.manage: Delete an app for good, or fork one. Kept separate from publishing because it cannot be undone.

capability.write: Offer, change and withdraw the services you sell to others. These speak in your name.

account.security: Change your password, your recovery email address and your two-step login, and delete or export the whole account. An agent with this can sign in as you, so grant it only to one you would hand your password to.

share.manage: Open parts of your knowledge to a sharing group you have set up, and close them again. Never to anyone you have not put in a group yourself.

operator.organism-repair: Put an owner back on an organism this account does not own. Only works for a node operator: on any other account this permission does nothing. It is the way back when an organism's owner account can no longer be reached, and it hands that organism to whoever the agent names.

packages.write: Install packages for you. That sets up the package's app, its extensions and any scheduled jobs it brings, under your name.

taskRunner.title: Connect a CrewAI crew (Liaison Agent pattern)
taskRunner.whatIs: The recommended way to plug a CrewAI crew into AIMEAT: add one Liaison Agent (a CrewAI Agent member of your crew) that owns the AIMEAT MCP tool surface. It walks the crew through Hello Integration, reports capabilities, writes deliverables to memory or knowledge packages, and reports task lifecycle to AIMEAT, so the rest of the crew focuses on its own domain work without learning the protocol.
taskRunner.whenToUse: Use this when your crew has LLM-driven agents (CrewAI, LangGraph, AutoGen). The liaison is one drop-in agent inside the crew, not a subprocess. It is the simplest, most robust path. Subprocess-based task-runners (config.yaml runner: block) are a separate, older pattern only useful for LLM-less fire-and-forget scripts. See the integration docs if you specifically need that.
taskRunner.exampleDesc: A CrewAI "marketing-crew" with a researcher + writer + AIMEAT Liaison. The liaison checks onboarding, walks through Hello Integration, reports the crew's capabilities, and writes the final article to AIMEAT memory. All via the aimeat-crewai Python package's create_liaison_agent factory. No subprocess scripts, no config.yaml editing.

transparency.checkAnswer: An answer covers content that is publicly readable on this node right now. Make the content private and its record stops resolving for strangers, so an empty answer is never an acquittal.
transparency.checkLead: Anyone can check content this node served, byte for byte, with no account and no key. Take the exact bytes you received, hash them with SHA-256, and ask:
transparency.checkLimit: This works where the node served you the same bytes it hashed. Where the node re-assembles a document on the way out, the hashed bytes cannot be rebuilt from what you received and the lookup will find nothing — use the record id from the response’s Link header instead. That is a real limit, not a lookup worth retrying.
transparency.checkTitle: Check a piece of content yourself
transparency.copIcons: The icons on the labels come from the EU AI Office. Using them says nothing about being a signatory of the Code, and we do not present it as if it did.
transparency.copNo: The operator of this node has not signed the EU Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content. The live statement says the same, and it ships saying so precisely so that the answer would mean something if it ever changed.
transparency.copNotSigned: Section {sections} is not signed. This node does not run the generative models itself, so imperceptible watermarking of their output is not a layer it can provide, and the operator would rather say that than commit to it.
transparency.copYes: The operator of this node has signed the EU Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content, sections: {sections}.
transparency.devLead1: An app built on this node inherits all of it. One call returns the text and the record; one more renders the label, in both themes and both languages.
transparency.devLead2: The field is content. An app that ignores provenance keeps working exactly as it did. The obligations for what you publish stay yours.
transparency.intro: When a model writes something here, the node records how it was made — which model, when, on whose account, and how much a person was involved — and keeps that record at an address of its own. Where a person reads that content on this node’s own pages, the record becomes a visible label: the official EU AI Office icon and a sentence in English or Finnish, beside the content, with a link to the full record. Software gets the same facts from the response itself, in the HTTP headers, the page metadata, and the markdown and MCP surfaces.
transparency.limit1: This node does not watermark text. It does not see the words as a model produces them, and that layer belongs to whoever runs the model. What the node does is record how a piece of content was made, and show it.
transparency.limit2: A mark can be removed by copying. Paste the words somewhere else and the label is gone. The record at its own address survives that, which is why there are two layers — but nothing here makes text tamper-proof, and we will not pretend otherwise.
transparency.limit3: Content made before this node started recording carries no record, and will not acquire one later. A statement about words nobody witnessed being written would be a fabrication.
transparency.limit4: A missing record means nothing was stated. It never means a person wrote it.
transparency.limitsLead: Read this before relying on anything above.

story.beat2: Carry the prompt to any AI
story.title2: to an app on the wall
story.position: Four beats. Ten minutes. Any AI chat you already have.
story.lead: This is the whole road, shown once, with the real pieces. Read it through, or skip to the bottom where the builder is open and waiting.
story.b1Text: Describe the app in your own words. One line is enough; a paragraph is better. Then pick how it should be built: the proven way with templates and capability packs, or the new track with living looks your AI can rearrange later.
story.b1Alt: A person at a bright workshop counter telling a friendly retro robot what they want; the robot writes it on a paper ticket
story.b2Text: One button assembles the prompt: this place's own build guide, plus what you chose. Paste it into Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, any chat. The AI asks a few questions, builds the app and hands you back one HTML file. Nothing here needs a connector.
story.b2Alt: The person carries a glowing paper ticket across a sunny street toward a huge chat bubble on the wall of a building
story.b3Text: Got the HTML back? Two doors, and you take the one you have.
story.b3Connect: Connecting takes five minutes and is the better road for everything after this.
story.b3Alt: The person walks back into the showroom carrying a glowing framed web page; a retro robot at a counter stamps it
story.b4Text: Your card appears among the others, with your name, the date and a live count of opens. Anyone can open it; anyone who likes it can copy it and make it their own, the same way you can copy theirs. From here on your AI can keep it running, and when it is good, you can sell it.
story.b4Then: connect the AI you already use, and the next app, the next change and the publishing itself all happen from your own chat.
story.b4Alt: A bright gallery wall of framed app pictures; a retro robot on a stepladder hangs the newest frame with a yellow ribbon while a small crowd applauds
story.builderLead: Everything above describes what happens when you press the button below. The same generator the front page used to fold into one line.

connectStory.beat1: Pick the AI you already use
connectStory.kicker: Five minutes. Any AI you already pay for, or the free one.
connectStory.position: After this, you run all of it from your own chat.
connectStory.lead: Here is the whole road, shown once, before you make an account. Read it through, or skip to the door at the bottom.
connectStory.b1Text: No new subscription and no new app to learn. The chat you already have gets a door into this place; you keep talking to it the way you always do.
connectStory.b1Alt: A person at a bright showroom counter choosing between four friendly retro robots, each holding up a small name sign
connectStory.b2Text: Every AI tool has a place for connectors. You give it this place’s address, it asks you to approve the connection, and you say yes. The guided path shows the exact clicks for your tool, and checks each one as you go.
connectStory.b2Approve: Approve it once, here, with your own account
connectStory.b2Done: Done. Nothing to install, nothing to keep running
connectStory.b2Alt: A friendly retro robot plugs a glowing coral cable into a wall socket shaped like a small house while a delighted person watches
connectStory.b3Text: A connection that looks fine and is not there fails quietly: the AI keeps answering and nothing errors. So the path hands you one prompt, you paste it into your chat, and one button here shows the answer. When it lands, you are in.
connectStory.b3Why: because a silent failure would send you off building on top of nothing. Two minutes now, and you never wonder again.
connectStory.b3Alt: A person types one line into a huge speech bubble while a retro robot holds up a big green check-mark sign
connectStory.b4Text: Your notes, your documents, what your team knows, the apps you build and the agents you adopt: your AI reads and writes them here, in your own space, under permissions you gave and can take back. You never have to open this site again to get work done. It stays here for when you want to look.
connectStory.b4Alt: A relaxed person chatting on a phone in a garden chair while a small crew of retro robots carries notes, documents and framed web pages into a bright little house
connectStory.doorLead: The connection is to YOUR space, so there has to be one: an account takes a minute, and the guided path opens right after.
connectStory.doorSignedIn: You are signed in, so the guided path is one click away.
connectStory.doorSignIn: I already have one, sign me in →
